hmmt-feb-2004-calc-01.title: Use continuity
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-01.body:
For fixed $x=\pi\neq0$ the expression $\frac{f(x+h)-f(h)}{x}$ is continuous in $h$, so the limit as $h\to0$ is obtained by substituting $h=0$: $\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x}$.

At $x=\pi$: $\frac{\sin(\sin\pi)-\sin(\sin0)}{\pi}=\frac{\sin0-\sin0}{\pi}=0$.

**Answer: 0**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-02.title: Telescoping
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-02.body:
Let $g(x)=f(x)-f(2x)$. Then $f(x)-f(4x)=(f(x)-f(2x))+(f(2x)-f(4x))=g(x)+g(2x)$.

Its derivative is $g'(x)+2g'(2x)$, which at $x=1$ is $g'(1)+2g'(2)=5+2\cdot7=19$.

**Answer: 19**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-03.title: Difference of cubes
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-03.body:
Write $u=\sqrt[3]{x^3+x^2}$, $v=\sqrt[3]{x^3-x^2}$. Then $u^3-v^3=2x^2$ and
$$u-v=\frac{2x^2}{u^2+uv+v^2}.$$
Since $u=x\left(1+\tfrac1x\right)^{1/3}$ and $v=x\left(1-\tfrac1x\right)^{1/3}$, both $u/x,v/x\to1$, so $u^2+uv+v^2\sim3x^2$ and the limit is $\frac{2}{3}$.

**Answer: $\frac23$**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-04.title: Chain rule
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-04.body:
Let $f_0(x)=x$ and $f_n(x)=\cos f_{n-1}(x)$. By induction $f_n(a)=a$ and $f_n'(a)=(-\sin a)^n$: indeed $f_n'(a)=-\sin(f_{n-1}(a))\cdot f_{n-1}'(a)=(-\sin a)(-\sin a)^{n-1}$.

So $f'(a)=f_8'(a)=\sin^8a=(\sin^2a)^4=(1-\cos^2a)^4=(1-a^2)^4$, since $\cos a=a$.

Expanding: $f'(a)=a^8-4a^6+6a^4-4a^2+1$.

**Answer: $a^8-4a^6+6a^4-4a^2+1$**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-05.title: Polar integral
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-05.body:
At $30$ rpm the turntable turns $\pi$ radians in $1$ second. If the mouse waits until the turntable has turned through angle $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ and then launches, he can drive along that ray for the remaining $1-\theta/\pi$ seconds, reaching any point on the ray up to distance $r(\theta)=1-\theta/\pi$ from the centre. Waiting for an angle beyond $\pi$ is impossible, and these rays (with all shorter distances) fill out $S$.

The area is the polar integral
$$\int_0^\pi\frac{r(\theta)^2}{2}\,d\theta=\frac12\int_0^\pi\left(1-\frac\theta\pi\right)^2d\theta=\frac1{2\pi^2}\int_0^\pi\varphi^2\,d\varphi=\frac{1}{2\pi^2}\cdot\frac{\pi^3}{3}=\frac\pi6.$$
(with $\varphi=\pi-\theta$).

**Answer: $\frac{\pi}{6}$ square meters**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-06.title: Logarithmic differentiation
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-06.body:
Let $g(x)=\ln f(x)=x\ln x$. Then $\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}=g'(x)=1+\ln x$.

So $f'(x)=f(x)$ (note $f(x)>0$) exactly when $1+\ln x=1$, i.e. $x=1$.

**Answer: 1**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-07.title: Integrate $|y|$ bound
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-07.body:
The condition is $y^2\le x^2-x^6$, i.e. $|y|\le\sqrt{x^2-x^6}=|x|\sqrt{1-x^4}$ for $|x|\le1$.

Area $=\displaystyle2\int_{-1}^{1}|x|\sqrt{1-x^4}\,dx=4\int_0^1x\sqrt{1-x^4}\,dx$. With $u=x^2$, $du=2x\,dx$ this is $2\int_0^1\sqrt{1-u^2}\,du=2\cdot\frac\pi4=\frac\pi2$.

**Answer: $\frac\pi2$**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-08.title: Implicit differentiation
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-08.body:
The curve $(x+y)^4=x-y$ is bounded above in $y$ (see below), so the maximum occurs where $\frac{dy}{dx}=0$. Differentiating: $4(1+y')(x+y)^3=1-y'$. Setting $y'=0$ gives $4(x+y)^3=1$, so $x+y=\frac1{\sqrt[3]4}=\frac{\sqrt[3]2}{2}$.

Then $x-y=(x+y)^4=(x+y)\cdot(x+y)^3=\frac{\sqrt[3]2}{2}\cdot\frac14=\frac{\sqrt[3]2}{8}$.

Subtracting, $2y=\frac{\sqrt[3]2}2-\frac{\sqrt[3]2}8=\frac{3\sqrt[3]2}{8}$, so $y=\frac{3\sqrt[3]2}{16}$.

(The curve is a rotated and scaled copy of $y=x^4$, so it has a single highest point, which is this critical point.)

**Answer: $\frac{3\sqrt[3]{2}}{16}$**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-08.title: Substitution
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-08.body:
Let $s=x+y$, $t=x-y$, so $t=s^4$ and $y=\frac{s-t}{2}=\frac{s-s^4}{2}$. Maximise $h(s)=\frac{s-s^4}2$ over real $s$: $h'(s)=\frac{1-4s^3}{2}=0$ gives $s^3=\frac14$, a maximum since $h\to-\infty$ as $|s|\to\infty$. Then $h=\frac{s(1-s^3)}{2}=\frac{s\cdot\frac34}{2}=\frac{3s}{8}=\frac{3}{8\sqrt[3]4}=\frac{3\sqrt[3]2}{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{3\sqrt[3]{2}}{16}$**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-09.title: Ratio test
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-09.body:
The ratio of consecutive terms is
$$\frac{(n+1)!/(c(n+1))^{n+1}}{n!/(cn)^n}=\frac{n+1}{c(n+1)}\left(\frac{n}{n+1}\right)^n=\frac1c\left(1+\frac1n\right)^{-n}\to\frac{1}{ce}.$$
The series converges when $\frac1{ce}<1$, i.e. $c>\frac1e$, and diverges when $c<\frac1e$. So $c_0=\frac1e$.

**Answer: $\frac1e$**

hmmt-feb-2004-calc-10.title: Symmetry $P(1-x)=1-P(x)$
hmmt-feb-2004-calc-10.body:
With $u=x-\frac12$ we get $P(x)-\frac12=u^3+\frac u4$, an odd function of $u$. Replacing $x$ by $1-x$ replaces $u$ by $-u$, so $P(1-x)=1-P(x)$. Then by induction $P^{[k]}(1-x)=1-P^{[k]}(x)$ for all $k$.

Let $I=\int_0^1P^{[2004]}(x)\,dx$. Substituting $x\to1-x$:
$$I=\int_0^1P^{[2004]}(1-x)\,dx=\int_0^1\bigl(1-P^{[2004]}(x)\bigr)dx=1-I.$$
So $I=\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**
